dietary intakes of dairy products, dietary calcium and vitamin D, and dietary vitamin D supplements were each inversely related to risk of incident hypertension in middle-aged women.
intake of low-fat dairy, but not high-fat dairy products, was associated with a lower risk of hypertension in a large prospective cohort of middle-aged and older US women.
intakes of dairy products and their nutrient components, calcium and vitamin D, were inversely associated with the incidence of high blood pressure in middle-aged and elderly women.

the associations of dairy products and their components, calcium, and Vitamin D, with the risk of hypertension in a large prospective cohort of US women.
the relationship between intake of dairy foods, calcium and vitamin D and the incidence of hypertension.
the associations between dietary calcium, vitamin D, and low-fat dairy product consumption and the risk of incident hypertension.

dairy products and calcium and vitamin D intake are associated with lower risk of hypertension in women, but the association of high-fat dairy intake with hypertension remains unclear.
low-fat dairy product consumption is associated with a reduced risk of hypertension in women, but high-fat dairy consumption is not.
the intake of low-fat dairy, calcium, and/or vitamin D was not associated with the incidence of high blood pressure in this study.

the consumption of low-fat dairy, calcium, and especially vitamin D, are associated with a reduced risk of developing hypertension.
low-fat dairy products are associated with lower risk of hypertension, and this association was partly explained by the calcium content.

dairy intake may be beneficial to cardiovascular health, especially in women.
